item.title: Did These Scientists Find Evidence of Blood in a Dinosaur Bone?
item.description: Mineralized “structures” discovered in the bone were the fossilized remains of red blood cells, according to a recent study. Other experts aren’t so sure.
item.dc:creator: Stella Raine Chu
item.category: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
item.media:description: Fossilized remains from a hind limb of the dinosaur Aratasaurus at the Museu de Paleontologia Plácido Cidade Nuvens in Brazil.

item.title: NASA Is Selecting Future Astronauts. Here’s How to Apply.
item.description: The space agency is recruiting its next class of space travelers for missions to low-Earth orbit and the moon. Applications are due Dec. 3.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:description: The new recruits would most likely participate in the Artemis program, which flew its first crewed mission, a loop around the moon, in April.

item.title: Top Astrophysicist Leaves U.S. After Trump Policies Affect Her Work
item.description: Kelly Holley-Bockelmann was one of the top astrophysicists in the country until President Trump’s policies affected every part of her work.
item.dc:creator: Eli Saslow and Hilary Swift
item.media:credit: Hilary Swift for The New York Times

item.title: Still on the President’s Agenda: Daylight Saving Time
item.description: Following an election-year rout for Republicans, Trump castigated lawmakers for not passing the Sunshine Protection Act. Some scientists have warned against the change.
item.dc:creator: Lynne Peeples
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross for The New York Times
item.media:description: If the president were to sign a bill making daylight saving time permanent, most clocks in the U.S. could suddenly spring forward, pushing sunrise to after 9 a.m. in many places for several weeks.

item.title: What a Democratic Congress Could Mean for Science
item.description: The Trump administration has sought to reshape the nation’s research infrastructure. Democratic lawmakers, newly empowered, are preparing to push back.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Mueller, Carolyn Y. Johnson, Cade Metz and Kenneth Chang
item.media:credit: Kristina Barker for The New York Times
item.media:description: Preparing to redeploy a National Science Foundation data-gathering buoy in the Pacific last month after the Trump administration ordered the network of ocean monitors dismantled earlier this year.

item.title: These Newly Elected Lawmakers Know Something Trump Doesn’t: Science
item.description: Among those elected to Congress on Tuesday are a mathematician, a microbiologist and a chemical engineer. They plan to take on a White House that has threatened funding cuts to research.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Nazaryan
item.media:credit: E. Jason Wambsgans/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service, via Getty Images
item.media:description: Daniel K. Biss earned a Ph.D. in mathematics at M.I.T. and taught math at the University of Chicago before moving to politics, first as an Illinois state legislator and, since 2021, as the mayor of Evanston.

item.title: Biotech Firm Claims Some Credit for Groundbreaking Virus Research
item.description: Radical Numerics turned heads with its announcement about a novel treatment. Now a former partner, Tabula Bioscience, says it performed much of the research.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer
item.media:credit: Ben Pennington/The Boston Globe, via Getty Images
item.media:description: George Church, a prominent geneticist at Harvard, resigned as an adviser to Radical Numerics over concerns that it had presented experimental results produced by another company as its own.

item.title: How A.I. Just Blew Up a Key Tenet of Computer Science
item.description: A longstanding hypothesis held that some problems would always be hard for computers to solve quickly. But OpenAI disproved it — raising the possibility of radical new efficiencies.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz

item.title: Were These Ancient Siberian Nomads the First Stoners?
item.description: Scientists ran a drug test on hair found in a 2,800-year-old burial mound. It came back positive for pot, the earliest known evidence of psychoactive cannabis use.
item.dc:creator: Annie Roth

item.title: A Guide to COP31 Climate Talks in Antalya, Turkey
item.description: Negotiators and leaders are gathering for annual United Nations climate talks. They come as global temperatures are set to breach a key threshold.
item.dc:creator: Chico Harlan
item.category: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
item.media:description: The entrance to the Antalya Expo, venue of the COP31 climate talks that begin on Monday in Turkey.

item.title: With Hopes Low and Temperatures High, Climate Summit Opens in Turkey
item.description: War, artificial intelligence and the Trump era have overshadowed climate change. But officials from nearly every nation are meeting to confront global warming.
item.dc:creator: Chico Harlan
item.category: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
item.media:description: A sign advertised the upcoming United Nations climate summit at the Istanbul airport in Turkey, which will host the meeting starting on Monday.

item.title: How an Intern and a Biologist Rescued an Orphaned Walrus in Alaska
item.description: An injured five-month-old walrus huddled next to carcasses in remote Alaska after it became separated from its mother. Humans came to its rescue.
item.dc:creator: Ishani Desai

item.title: How Cardiologists’ High Hopes for Two Drugs Were Dashed
item.description: By every measure, the drugs were no better than placebos, full data revealed on Saturday. Was it the fault of the design of the studies, or our very hypotheses about heart disease?
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata

item.title: Lonnie Thompson Has Died. He Dodged Avalanches to Preserve Climate History.
item.description: His observations helped establish shriveling mountain glaciers as an unmistakable consequence of human-caused warming. He was 78.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong

item.title: Disaster-Prone Communities Face Cuts and Slowdowns in Federal Help
item.description: The Trump administration is scaling back or stalling investments that help vulnerable places harden themselves to rising flood and fire threats.
item.dc:creator: Scott Dance
item.media:description: An apartment complex in Milton, Fla., in October, after Hurricane Isaias.

item.title: Environmental Ballot Wins
item.description: Voters around the country approved measures on conservation, water and data centers on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Scott Dance
item.media:description: A protest outside the municipal building in Kenilworth, N.J., in October.

item.title: Tiny Chihuahuas Hold a Big Surprise: A Sliver of Coyote DNA
item.description: The breed is descended from indigenous canines, which may have been intentionally mixed with wild coyotes long before Europeans arrived in the Americas.
item.dc:creator: Franz Lidz

item.title: Beverly Whipple Has Died. She Introduced the G-Spot to the Mainstream.
item.description: Dr. Whipple studied the female erogenous zone and, with collaborators, wrote a best seller about women’s sexuality. She was 85.
item.dc:creator: Randi Hutter Epstein
item.category: The G Spot and Other Recent Discoveries About Human Sexuality (Book)
item.media:description: Beverly Whipple in 2007. Her book “The G Spot: And Other Recent Discoveries About Human Sexuality,” examined the concept of female sexual pleasure.

item.title: Prosecutors Seek to Drop Charges Against Russian Scientist Accused of Smuggling Frog Embryos
item.description: Kseniia Petrova, a researcher at Harvard, has argued that she was vindictively prosecuted after her arrest in 2025.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson
item.media:description: Kseniia Petrova, a Russian-born scientist at Harvard, seen after she was released from U.S. federal custody in Boston in 2025.

item.title: A NASA Telescope Has Crashed Back to Earth
item.description: The space agency estimated that there was a one-in-2,100 chance that debris from the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory could injure someone on the ground.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:description: Preparing the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory for launch at the Kennedy Space Center in 2004. The 1.5-ton spacecraft is about the size of a pickup truck.

item.title: The Election Day Edition
item.description: In the 2022 midterms, Democrats made global warming an issue. Things have changed.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer

item.title: House Republicans Accuse Top Psychology Group of Antisemitism
item.description: A monthslong G.O.P. effort culminated in a scathing report about emails and other exchanges within the American Psychological Association.
item.dc:creator: Christina Caron and Azeen Ghorayshi
item.category: Brandeis, Louis D, Center for Human Rights Under Law
item.media:description: Representative Tim Walberg, Republican of Michigan, led the House committee whose recent report accused the American Psychological Association of antisemitism.

item.title: The Southwest Is Parched. Can the Recent Floodwaters Quench It?
item.description: A series of storms has added to reservoirs in the Colorado River basin, but the long-term water outlook remains bleak.
item.dc:creator: Scott Dance
item.media:description: A mud-covered street after flooding in Durango, Colo., on Monday.

item.title: Neanderthals Used Wood for Tools, Housing — and Murder?
item.description: In one case, 75,000-year-old bones reveal what may be the earliest identifiable victim of death by wooden spear.
item.dc:creator: Franz Lidz
item.media:description: Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan has long anchored the scientific argument for complex Neanderthal cognition.

item.title: Investigators Looking for Cause of Learjet Crash Say Ice Was ‘Certainly a Factor’
item.description: Ice, experts said, can change the shape of a plane’s wing, disrupting its aerodynamics.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Nazaryan
item.media:description: Police and other investigators on Monday at the scene of the plane crash in Greenacres, Fla.

item.title: Do Animals Grieve?
item.description: The feeling of existential loss was long thought to be uniquely human. But studies of coyotes, cockatoos and other creatures are prompting some scientists to reconsider.
item.dc:creator: Emily Anthes
item.media:credit: Loren Elliott for The New York Times

item.title: Why Did Snakes Lose Their Legs? And 9 More Animal Mysteries
item.description: There are more than 1.5 million known zoological species on Earth, with at least as many enigmas. Here are our top 10.
item.dc:creator: Emily Anthes and Stella Raine Chu
